title: The Count

facts.fact: Instead of going straight to the hall he went along the wall-walk after Wren, kept her count of the hall's lamps, nine, while she told him how stupid giving his name was, and promised to tell her first the next time he means to be brave.
facts.evidence: I'll tell you first.

facts.fact: On the wall-walk she counted the grey cloaks for him, five round the fire and one at the winch-house, and told him that among eleven wounded men and him he had been one in twelve, and now he was one in one.
facts.evidence: Now it's one in one.

facts.fact: She says it is a hundred and twelve paces from the gatehouse stair to the tower door, and she ran them so the bell would ring before anyone found him.
facts.evidence: A hundred and twelve paces from the gatehouse stair to the tower door.

facts.fact: She made him count the hall's lamps while she told him how stupid giving his name had been, a chit if he lost the count; he kept it, and her lips moved along the windows and stopped where his had.
facts.evidence: Lose the count and you owe me a chit.

facts.fact: She told him to tell her first, next time he means to be brave, so she doesn't run; when he said he would, she said he wouldn't, and wrote in her ledger: Times the Captain has promised to tell me first: 1.

recap: In the hour before dusk the grey cloaks climbed to the gate, and Confessor Ivo Marrant read his list to the House, Darrow's name first. Two of his men came through the wicket before Old Mercy rang, late, and Darrow's shoulder could not shut it. The Prior spoke the law of names, and Marrant made his camp on the lower terrace to wait for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel. Darrow went to the bars and gave him his name and his face.

facts.fact: He went to the Prior in the chapel for the reproach she had not given him; she answered in questions, and told him he is in the names she says every night, and was before he gave his to the Confessor.
facts.evidence: You were in it before you gave him your name.

facts.fact: Every night, alone in the chapel, she says the names of everyone under the House's roof, and notices which ones she has had to stop saying.
facts.evidence: Everyone under this roof, every night

facts.fact: Asked to be angry that Darrow buried the House's story at the gate, she asked whose story it was: he gave it to the lay brothers, she only let them carry it, and a lie told for a man is his to bury.
facts.evidence: A lie told for a man is his to bury

facts.fact: She told him the Menders' vow is four words, to mend what climbs, and nobody who wrote it thought to add 'and hand it down to whoever asks'; she has never once given a name to a writ.
facts.evidence: To mend what climbs.

facts.fact: She said she held the bell so that Darrow would have a choice too, and that he is in her count of names, and was before he gave his name to the Confessor.
facts.evidence: I held the bell so that you would have one too.

people.did: Alone in the chapel at night with one candle, saying the names of everyone under her roof, until the Captain came for a reproach and got questions instead.
people.now: Prior of Saint Ysolde's, with Confessor Ivo Marrant camped on the lower terrace below her gate. She let him read his list at the bars, and when he held his paper out under the law of guests she kept him waiting for the bell as long as she could, then had the wicket opened; two grey cloaks came through it before Old Mercy rang, late, and she spoke the law of names. When Darrow gave his name at the bars and the House's story died at her gate, the Confessor thanked her for her candour. She did not reproach Darrow; she asked whether his shoulder was hurt. That night in the chapel she told him a lie told for a man is his to bury, that she says the names of everyone under her roof every night, and that she has never once given a name to a writ; he is in her count.

quote.text: I have never once given a name to a writ. Did you think I would start with yours?

story_so_far.mother-ione: When the grey cloaks were sighted on the Holloway, the news went first to Mother Ione. She called a council in the warming room off the cloister: Maelis, Sister Pell, Rae Thorne who had heard the list read, and Darrow, whose name is first on it. She asked how it was read, had the law of Old Mercy said aloud for the Captain, and asked Sister Pell whether she would ring it dawn and dusk for as long as the grey cloaks wait. The council broke with nothing decided aloud, and she called Darrow back to ask what she ought to know before she decides. At the next dawn bell she came to the foot of Darrow's cot: the winch-brothers had taken his far side of the mountain down to the valley, Old Mercy had not rung at dusk, so the valley heard what it always hears from the House, and when the grey cloaks are at the bars he is to tell Wren when. In the hour before dusk she stood before the gate and let the Confessor read; she kept him waiting at the wicket for the bell as long as the law of guests allowed, and when his men came through and the bell rang late, she gave him the law's other half, that no name under it is taken down against its will. When Darrow gave his name at the bars, the Confessor thanked her for her candour, and she asked Darrow only whether the shoulder was hurt.

facts.fact: After the night bell he went down the hall to the three Ninth men read with him at the gate with an order, to go on not knowing him, and said he would tell the Confessor himself they were not his; the oldest called it deciding for them without asking, and Darrow let the order go and asked what they wanted.

On the night of the gate he believed it was mercy that his name was not read, and said good night to the Captain. At the dawn bell of the feast his lips did not move: he lay breathing, slow and even, his eyes open on the roof and frost on his mouth, Hollowed. story_so_far.benedek-orrin: A knight of the Sixth Lance who came back from Harrow Ford with a boar spear wound through the shoulder and a fever after it, and has the cot next to Hollis Garrow's at Saint Ysolde's. He says his oath at every bell. On the morning the grey cloaks were seen on the Holloway he asked Hollis what it meant to be second on the list, offered to carry him down the Steps himself if they would let him, and was told he couldn't carry a bucket, which made him smile. Hollis told him to say his oath and shut his eyes, and he did.
story_so_far.maelis-vorne: She met Darrow at the gate of Saint Ysolde's when the lay brothers carried him up the Steps, read his knee with two fingers and her eyes shut, and named it not broken but undone. She would not touch it for six weeks, then sat on the end of his cot with a wooden box on her knees and offered him two ways off the mountain: the Crown's, which is fast, or hers, which is made of him and can't be taken back. When he chose hers, she bound the knee with emberthread, an old art she asked him never to mention she practices. Seven weeks on she still reads the Knots, has said no fourteen times when he asked to go down the Steps, and has warned him that the soft season is now and that the quiet in the knee is a liar. Then Wren brought word of six riders in grey cloaks on the Holloway and of a list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's read out at the inn in Coldmere; asked who was first on it, Wren only looked at Darrow. At the gate she stood behind the Prior while the list was read, and the Confessor's eyes found her and stayed; afterwards, when he had given his name at the bars, she told him a hidden man is a lie they find in the end and a named one is a law they must break where the valley can watch, and to keep it that way.
story_so_far.wren-ashdown: She counted the Thousand Steps aloud beside Darrow's litter on the day the lay brothers carried him up to Saint Ysolde's, insisting there are eleven hundred and seventeen and that everyone who says a thousand is wrong. Her ledgers keep the House's tallies: the Steps, the cots, the bells, and how many times the captain of the Ninth has asked to go down the mountain and how many times Mender Vorne has said no. Seven weeks after the Binding, on the first snow of the year, she came down from the bell tower to the infirmary hall, out of breath, with word of six grey cloaks and a censer on the Holloway road, and of a list read out at the inn in Coldmere naming the Faithless they had come to bring down to kneel. Hollis is second on it. When he asked who was first, she looked at Darrow. When they came in three bells early she was on the gate wall with Pell's glass, counting them, until the last was in and she had no number for it. At the gate she stood at the Captain's side while his name was read, and ran for the bell tower on his word. When he gave his name at the bars anyway, she counted the Confessors instead of looking at him.

title: The Far Lamp

facts.fact: He sat the far lamp after the night bell with the night novice, told her he did not know whether it would come again, and kept the lamp himself when she fell asleep.
facts.evidence: I don't know.

facts.fact: Asked what a watch is when you can do nothing, he said: you keep the lamp, you keep the count, and in the morning you can tell them true.
facts.evidence: you can tell them true

people.did: Keeping the far lamp at night while the night novice sleeps, his fingers black with wick soot.
people.now: He has answered to his name: he gave it and his rank to the Confessor at the bars in front of the whole House, and the valley's story is dead at the gate. Maelis read the knee after the wicket and found it held, and still soft; the word under his name has changed on his palms. On the night of the gate he went down the hall to his three Ninth men and came back having promised they would be asked before he decides for them again, and he won a story told true off Hollis at knucklebones. On the feast morning Benedek lay Hollowed in the next cot but one, frost on his mouth and a chip of black glass under his tongue that the far cots never had. Darrow held the hall's eyes on the lad's mouth, not the door, and from his cot learned that nobody passed in the night. Confessor Ivo Marrant and four grey cloaks sit up in turns round one fire on the lower terrace below the gate, the sixth keeps the winch-house. After the finding he asked Maelis what the glass was and got no answer; instead she made him say what he feared, that the bell's law cannot protect a man who has no will to refuse with, and ordered him to take the slow way every time. He got Hollis to eat the feast bread by holding the lad's hand for the length of a loaf, and owes Hollis silence about how. The day after the feast he learned from his cot that nobody passed in the night (the novice at the far lamp, the kitchen's flour, Wren's count of doors and keys) and told the hall so before the Confessor's word, ember witchcraft, could settle on Maelis. That evening he found the kitchen's book taking odds on who is Hollowed next, himself at five to one, and bet the kitchen ovens on nobody. That night he sat the far lamp with the night novice and kept it alone once she slept.

people.did: At the Grey Cot after the night bell with the lad's hand in his, talking to him too low to carry.
people.now: In the infirmary hall of Saint Ysolde's, second on the list Confessor Ivo Marrant read at the bars. He is dry, which he has told the Captain and nobody else. On the night of the gate, over knucklebones, he told the Captain that for a moment at the window he had wanted him to go down and kneel for the rest, and swore to say such thoughts aloud. At the dawn bell of the feast Benedek, of his own Sixth, lay Hollowed in the next cot; Hollis took the lad's hand in both of his and said it out loud: he had told the lad to get some sleep. He let the Captain hold the lad's hand for the length of a feast loaf so he could eat with a hand that was never empty, then took it back; the Mender is to be told he ate, not how. The Confessors sit up in turns round their fire on the lower terrace below the gate. He sits the watch at the Grey Cot and would not let the lad be carried to the far cots.

story_so_far.darrow: With the Grace of the field-stone warm in his chest and sixty knights behind him, Darrow led the Ninth Lance into the Wend at Harrow Ford, laughing, until halfway across the warmth went out of him, his horse went down, and his knee gave with nothing touching it as he planted and turned toward the boy who had gone under his horse. As he went under he saw Aldric Vane's horse on the west bank, already turned and climbing out, one heartbeat early. A red-handed clanswoman hauled him onto the east bank by his collar and made him look: the Wend carrying knights downstream, the Second Lance sitting untouched on the far shore, and a line of grey armored figures standing very still under the trees. Nineteen of the Ninth came home, and the Crown's heralds were already on the bell-house steps naming them the Faithless and bidding them kneel anew at the Oathspire. Carried up the Thousand Steps to the House of Menders, he chose Maelis Vorne's old art over the Crown's fast way, a strand of his own sinew bound in with emberthread, nothing given and nothing anyone can take back, and heard that he may never kneel again. Seven weeks on, walking without the stick, he learns that six grey cloaks with a cart and a censer are riding the Holloway toward the foot of the Steps with a list of the Faithless, and that when Wren was asked who was first on it, she looked at him. He asked to be sent down the Steps before the grey cloaks came and was refused a fifteenth time; he told the Prior to let the valley hear that the Faithless had gone down the far side, and she held Old Mercy silent so the gate would look as if it kept nobody. From the gate wall he watched the grey cloaks come in at the winch-house three bells early, and in the hour before dusk he stood among the wounded in the court while Confessor Ivo Marrant read his name first. He read the Confessor's trap a breath before it sprang and sent Wren for the bell, but the bell rang late: two grey cloaks came through the wicket, and his shoulder could not shut it on a third. When the bell stopped them and the Prior spoke the law of names, the Confessor made his camp on the lower terrace and called for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel. Darrow crossed the court to the bars and gave him his name.
story_so_far.hollis-garrow: At Harrow Ford he brought the writ from command that sent the Sixth and the Ninth into the river, and when Darrow pointed at the carts and children behind the clan line he answered that the clans were stupid and told him to mount up. He came back from Harrow Ford on a cart, missing his right leg above the knee. On the five days of carts and barge back through the Lowmarch, with the Crown's heralds reading the proclamation of the Faithless from every bell-house, he cursed everything from the surgeon to himself and then went quiet. He has had the cot next to Darrow's at Saint Ysolde's since, mostly drunk through the weeks before the Binding, and now six grey cloaks and a censer are on the Holloway below with his name second on their list. When they came to the gate he had himself carried up to the gatehouse window to see the man who wanted him, heard his name read second, looked at the wax on the writ and away, and when the Captain gave his name at the bars, told him he had seen him move at it, that nobody else had, and called him Captain.

where.detail: the far end of the infirmary hall at night, on a stool beneath the lamp that is never let go out, keeping it while the night novice sleeps on her folded arms

last_beat: After the night bell Darrow went down to the far lamp and asked the night novice if he might sit it with her. "It's my lamp." She let him. "Will it come again?" "I don't know." She had put a wick on nobody; the kitchen had it at twelve by supper. "What do you do on a watch, when you can't do anything?" "You keep it. You keep the lamp, and you keep the count, and when somebody asks you in the morning, you can tell them true." The lamp man on his round saw the Captain on a stool and lost his count. The novice slept on her folded arms; Darrow kept the lamp, trimming it till his fingers were black in the creases, as hers had been.
season: first snow of the year on the Steps

quest.name: The List
quest.on_the_page: The Confessors have come for the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's with a list: Darrow first, Hollis second. The named are to be taken down the Steps to the Oathspire and made to kneel where everyone can watch, which would say the Ninth drowned for its own bad faith, and would tear the thread in Darrow's knee. What stands between them and the hall is Old Mercy, the sanctuary bell: while it rings at dawn and dusk, no blade passes the gate and no name under it is taken down against its will. Miss one ringing and the law lapses till the next, and Sister Pell, who rings it, is very old. At the gate, Confessor Ivo Marrant read his names at the bars, and two of his men came through the wicket before the bell rang, late. Now five grey cloaks are camped on the lower terrace below the gate, and the sixth holds the winch-house, the cage and Rae's cart, so the road is theirs. Marrant's price: the Captain of the Ninth comes down and kneels, and the rest of the paper goes back in his cloak. Darrow went to the bars and gave him his name and his face. Marrant says he will wait.

struggle: The soft season, and the waiting. The knee is held and still soft. Benedek lies Hollowed in the Grey Cot, and nobody passed in the night; the Confessor's word for it, ember witchcraft, has come up the Steps, and the hall wants a hand to fit it. Under it is the thing he has said only to Maelis: a lad who cannot answer has no will for the bell to keep.

set: a borrowed stick he refuses to use

facts.evidence: nobody had passed on his watch either

facts.fact: He would not take Pell's glass to watch Rae go down; he followed her hood with his own eyes, and his mouth moved with the count.
facts.evidence: Darrow did not take the glass

facts.fact: He asked Rae where the name Thorne came from.
facts.evidence: Where's that from?

facts.fact: Asked who the letter was from, he said he had not looked, and put it under the mattress with the wax whole.
facts.evidence: I haven't looked

facts.fact: At dusk the script came up on his palm unasked, and beside the lines he knew ran a new, finer one, counting, and not counting him alone.
facts.evidence: It was not counting him. Or not him alone.

facts.fact: From the flour Rae reported he read that the grey cloaks mean to stay the winter.
facts.evidence: They mean to winter, then.

facts.fact: He asked Rae who gave her the letter; she would not say.
facts.evidence: Who gave it you?

facts.fact: When Rae said her grandmother was Thornwild-born he thought of the Thornwild as he had last seen them, across the ford behind their spears, with their old people on the bedding in the carts.
facts.evidence: He had last seen the Thornwild across the ford

people.did: Went down the Steps for her oxen after the dawn bell and came up the Last Hundred at dusk with a letter in blue wax for the Captain of the Ninth; called him Darrow.
people.now: In the House for the night, with her oxen stabled in the winch-house byre under a grey cloak's eye. She calls him Darrow, not Ser, not Captain: she drives for the House, not the Ninth.

facts.fact: She took the Steps down without counting, like a road, and never looked back at the gate; at the winch-house she went to the near ox's head and stood there until the grey cloak got off her box.
facts.evidence: She went to the near ox's head and stood there

facts.fact: Her oxen are stabled in the winch-house byre with a grey cloak's stool in the door; the Confessors' cart has flour out of Coldmere for six men to the thaw and past it, and they bake it on the House's wood.
facts.evidence: for six men to the thaw and past it

facts.fact: The near ox is Hob: she said his name once, unasked, and nobody remarked on it.
facts.evidence: Hob won't eat with him there.

facts.fact: She brought up a letter in blue wax for the Captain of the Ninth at the House of Menders, and when he asked who gave it her she said only that it came up with her.
facts.evidence: It came up with me.

facts.fact: She called him Darrow, not Ser, not Captain: she does not drive for the Ninth, she drives for the House.
facts.evidence: I don't drive for the Ninth.

facts.fact: Her grandmother was Thornwild-born and came over the Wend behind a drover, long before the ford; Coldmere called the family the Thornwild woman's, and it wore down to Thorne, and they kept it.
facts.evidence: Coldmere called us the Thornwild woman's, and it wore down to Thorne.

facts.fact: When she told him her grandmother was Thornwild-born, she watched him take it.
facts.evidence: She watched him take that.

people.did: Counted Rae down the Steps aloud through Pell's glass, stretch by stretch, and saw the grey cloak get off the box for her.
people.now: On the gate wall at dawn with Pell's glass, lent and counted out again. She counts the Captain's steps for the Mender, and counted Rae's down the cliff at her; when the grey cloak got down she wrote nothing.

facts.fact: No writ names a carter, and the bell lets anybody down; coming back up is eleven hundred and seventeen steps.
facts.evidence: Coming back up's eleven hundred and seventeen.

facts.fact: She has watched Rae on the Steps: Rae never counts them, she takes them like a road.
facts.evidence: She takes them like a road.

facts.fact: When the grey cloak got down off the cart for Rae, Wren said so and did not write it down.
facts.evidence: Wren did not write it down.

people.did: At the Grey Cot without looking round, knew Darrow had come in with post and asked who from.
people.now: At the Grey Cot with the lad's hand in his, as he has been since the feast. He knows a letter came up for Darrow and that Darrow has not looked at it.

facts.fact: Without looking round from the Grey Cot he knew Darrow had come in with a letter, and asked who it was from.
facts.evidence: Letter, is it?

codex.name: The stretches of the Steps
codex.text: The lay brothers' names for the runs of the Thousand Steps, which Wren counts by. From the bottom: the Shins, steep from the winch-house; the Elbow, where the stair goes into the cloud; the Long Reach; and last, below the gate itself, the Last Hundred (Ch 2 Sc 4).

codex.name: Hob
codex.text: The near one of Rae Thorne's two oxen, the slow one; the first of their names she has said, once, unasked (Ch 2 Sc 4).

now.against: The grey cloaks hold the winch-house and the cage and have brought flour for the whole winter; a letter in blue wax for the Captain of the Ninth lies under his mattress unopened.

title: The Carter
last_beat: Rae's day at the foot of the Steps, before she came up at dusk: she put the letter inside her shirt, wax inward, told Hob she would tell Darrow he wouldn't eat, and started back up the Steps.

people.did: Went down to her oxen without counting the Steps, moved the grey cloak off her box by standing at Hob's head, read the Confessors' cart by its flour, took the blue-wax letter for the Captain of the Ninth from the grey cloak's hand and carried it up inside her shirt rather than leave it a night at the bottom of the cage.
people.now: In the House for the night, with the letter delivered and her oxen in the winch-house byre under a grey cloak's eye. She carried it up herself rather than leave it a night with him. She calls the Captain Darrow.

facts.fact: She does not count the Steps: counting is for Wren and for men with lists, and a road you count gets longer under you.
facts.evidence: Rae Thorne did not count the Steps at all.

facts.fact: At the winch-house she stood at Hob's head with her hand on his neck until the grey cloak got off her box with a little bow, and she let him think it was manners.
facts.evidence: she let him think it was manners

facts.fact: Her other ox is Dun.
facts.evidence: put his nose in her armpit

facts.fact: She read the Confessors' cart by what it ate: flour with the Coldmere mill's mark, for six men to the thaw and past it, and nobody brings that for a paper they mean to read at a gate and take home.
facts.evidence: Nobody brings flour past the thaw for a paper they mean to read at a gate and take home.

facts.fact: The grey cloak at the winch-house gave her the letter, saying the Captain of the Ninth twice with a smile, the way you say the name of a horse you have already bought.
facts.evidence: the way you say the name of a horse you have already bought

facts.fact: Rather than leave the letter a night at the bottom of the cage with him sitting over it, she put it inside her shirt and carried it up herself.
facts.evidence: She took it out of his hand and put it inside her shirt, wax inward.

facts.fact: Before she started up she told Hob she would tell Darrow he would not eat.
facts.evidence: I'll tell Darrow you wouldn't.

codex.name: Dun
codex.text: The off one of Rae Thorne's two oxen, beside Hob (Ch 2, Interlude).
